intro: This is the third movement of Haydn’s Symphony No. 94, the “Surprise”, a minuet marked Allegro molto, the same tempo marking Haydn gave the finale. In the Trio between the louder outer sections, the first violins and bassoon play together.

sections.label: A · Menuetto in G major, Allegro molto
sections.mNote: Flute, bassoon and first violins play the tune.

sections.label: B · Trio, first violins and bassoon
sections.mNote: The Trio stays in G major, marked piano.

sections.label: A′ · Minuet da capo, full orchestra
sections.mNote: Da capo repeat of the minuet’s opening tune

cues.title: Opening theme of the minuet
cues.text: Flute, bassoon and first violins play the minuet’s opening tune, which leaps through G major in crotchets. The marking is Allegro molto.
cues.evidence: Menuetto, bars 1–8: leading instruments, crotchet motion and tempo marking. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Minuet, Allegro molto
cues.text: Richard Wigmore called this the fastest and lustiest minuet in all Haydn’s symphonies, a rustic dance with an “oompah” accompaniment. The second half is more involved. Its phrases are irregular, it has touches of counterpoint, and a three-note figure recurs.
cues.evidence: Richard Wigmore, booklet for Howard Shelley’s recording of the London symphonies (Hyperion, 2009), on the Allegro molto minuet: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/44371-B.pdf

cues.title: Inverted figure in the Trio
cues.text: The rising quaver figure that closes the first half of the minuet returns inverted in the Trio.
cues.evidence: Score discussion of the Menuetto and Trio: the first-half cadential figure reappears inverted in the Trio. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Trio, violins and bassoon
cues.text: The Trio stays in G major and leaves out most of the winds. The first violins and a bassoon play the tune above the other strings, all marked piano. The first half falls into two phrases of four bars each.
cues.evidence: Menuetto, Trio: G major, strings and bassoon, piano, with a four-plus-four-bar first half. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Minuet and Trio, Orrin Howard
cues.text: Orrin Howard called the minuet “a true Austrian peasant dance”. He described the Trio at its centre as “delightfully subtle and dignified”.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard, LA Phil programme note: https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise

cues.title: Return of the Menuetto
cues.text: At the end of the Trio the score marks Da capo, and the minuet is played again from the beginning. The flute plays with the bassoon and violins once more, and the full orchestra plays forte.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, edited by Julius Rietz, pp. 30–34: Menuetto opening and Men. D.C. at the end of the Trio. Opening scoring also described at https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Minuet to Trio in G major
transitions.from: A · Menuetto in G major, Allegro molto
transitions.to: B · Trio, first violins and bassoon
transitions.how: The minuet closes over a held G in the bass. The Trio stays in G major and reduces the orchestra to strings and bassoon, marked piano. Its falling quaver figure reverses a rising figure from the minuet.
transitions.evidence: Menuetto, closing G pedal and Trio opening, described in the score discussion: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

transitions.title: Trio to Menuetto da capo
transitions.from: B · Trio, first violins and bassoon
transitions.to: A′ · Minuet da capo, full orchestra
transitions.how: The Trio closes in G major and is followed by the instruction Menuetto da capo. The opening returns in the same key, with the full orchestra at forte. Flute, bassoon and first violins again play the tune together.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, edited by Julius Rietz, pp. 30–34: G major Trio, da capo direction and forte Menuetto opening. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

source.title: Haydn, Symphony No. 94, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, ed. Rietz, plate 8876, [1855])
source.locator: Menuetto and Trio, printed pp. 30–34: full-orchestra dance, quiet strings and bassoon, then da capo.

timeline.note: Flute, bassoon and first violins lead the minuet over the full orchestra.
First violins and bassoon share the quiet Trio tune above the other strings.
Da capo. The full orchestra plays the minuet again, forte.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition and any editorial alterations are not identified in the recording sources.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Young lists CVE-48987-1 with the recording date 24 April 1929, DAHR lists CVE-48987 among the Boston Symphony Orchestra and Koussevitzky recordings of Symphony No. 94 made that day, and the Bolig discography assigns the Menuetto to that matrix. Commons’ 1 January 1929 is not a session day.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts, United States
fields.note: Young heads the 22 April 1929 session “Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts” and lists the 24 April retaken sides of the same symphony under that session; DAHR gives Symphony Hall, Boston for the Andante side CVE-48984. A separate place for the 24 April retakes is not given.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Young lists the symphony as released 9/29 on M-55 (7058/60), with later AM-55, DM-55, HMV and LP issues. The upstream transfer also names set M-55 (Internet Archive description), and DAHR places the Andante on disc 7059. The disc number of this movement’s sides is not stated; the side order (sides 1–2 movement I, sides 3–4 the Andante, sides 5–6 the Menuetto and Finale) suggests 7058 for movement I and 7060 for the Menuetto and Finale, but that allocation is inferred.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Young and Bolig agree on the matrix and take (one take issued of four made, per Young’s bracketed count). The DAHR matrix page could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Bob Varney — transfer from original Victor 78s

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was uploaded in December 2008, which is an upload date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Transfer from the original Victor 78 rpm set M-55 into one 20:48 file, from which the four movements were extracted as separate Commons files.
fields.note: The file lengths of the four Commons movements sum to the length of the Internet Archive file within about a second. The extraction procedure, stylus, playback curve, side-join locations and noise treatment are not documented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Haydn died in 1809. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to the Koussevitzky/Boston recording attributed to 1929, and the Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons public-domain licence URL, not treated here as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The programme’s pre-1963 European rule applies because the 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension; Young gives the release as September 1929, which supports first publication well before 1963. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence; US status is not established.

quote.text: The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I.
quote.source: London notebook, after his benefit concert on 4 May 1795; our translation

composer.background:
On 4 May 1795, Haydn gave a benefit concert at the King’s Theatre in London. The programme included his new D major Symphony, now numbered 104. Afterwards he wrote in his notebook: “The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I. I made four thousand gulden this evening. Such a thing can only be done in England.” He was sixty-three. He was a wheelwright’s son and had spent most of his adult life in the livery of a servant of the Esterházy family.

Haydn was born in Rohrau in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who played the harp by ear and sang; his mother had worked as a cook. At about six, Joseph left home for schooling in Hainburg. By 1740 he was a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. As a chorister he sang church music daily but received little instruction in composition. Performances outside the cathedral also gave him chances to get a meal. When his voice broke and he was dismissed in 1749, another musician, Johann Michael Spangler, took him into his family’s crowded room.
